title: Extension bootstrapping and sandboxing prototype
content:
Notes to self: rough exploration of a plugin bootstrap + sandboxing model that works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Goal: let customers and partners provide small, allowed extensions (WASM or JS isolates) that can be attached to routes for transformation, enrichment, or post-processing while preserving our security and perf guarantees.

Motivation / use cases:
- Customer-provided response-formatters (e.g., redact PII, map to internal schema) without shipping code to our control plane.
- Per-tenant plugins for enrichment (call internal CRM) in Dedicated/private where network egress is allowed.
- Partner connectors that transform streaming tokens (low-latency).
- Lightweight validation hooks (validate structured JSON output before release).

Constraints & principles:
- No plugin should be able to escalate access (no raw host access, no persistent network except allowed egress policy).
- Must work in three deployment modes with clear differences: Hosted (strict sandbox, no external network except allowed third-party integrations), Dedicated (tenant network egress allowed but mediated), Private (customer controls egress but we provide guidelines).
- Cold-starts must be bounded; warm pools or pre-warming for high-QPS routes.
- Observability + tracing: plugins must emit telemetry but cannot leak sensitive tokens.
- Attestation: plugins should present a manifest + signature; platform verifies signature and integrity before enabling.

High-level design sketches:

1) Packaging model
- Allowed formats: WASM (primary) and JS isolates (quick prototype).
- Package = {manifest.toml, wasm.bin, safe-config.json, signature.sig}
- Manifest fields: name, version, entry-symbol, capabilities-required (kv-read, kv-write, http-outbound, kms-access), resource-hints (vCPU-ms, memory-mb, max-requests/sec)

ASCII flow (simplified):

  client request -> route -> pre-filter -> plugin-host -> runtime (WASM isolate) -> post-filter -> response

Where plugin-host is a managed worker process that loads signed plugin artifacts in an isolate and enforces resource limits.

2) Handshake & registration (API sketch)
- POST /plugins/register  (admin-scoped)
  body: {manifest: base64, artifact_url: https://..., signature: base64, scope: route|tenant|global}
  returns: {id, status: pending}  (server side verifies signature, scans artifact)
- POST /plugins/attest/:id/approve  (internal operator approves after scans)
- POST /routes/:routeId/plugins/attach  {plugin_id, mode: inline|sidecar, config}  -> returns 200 or error

3) Runtime contract (what plugin can call)
- host.call('log', {level, msg})  -> structured log with plugin metadata (no raw headers)
- host.kv.get(key) / host.kv.put(key, value)  -> only if capability granted
- host.http.request({method, url, headers, body, egressPolicyId})  -> only allowed URLs per policy
- host.metrics.increment('counter.name', tags)
- host.secrets.get('kms:key:alias') -> only with kms capability and per-tenant allowlist
- host.emit_event({type, payload}) -> for audit trails (platform-level)

4) Resource limits & sandboxing
- CPU: cap per-request and global per-plugin. Time-budget enforced (e.g., 200ms on-request, adjustable by route config).
- Memory: max heap per isolate (e.g., 64MB default).
- Network: explicit egress allowlist + per-plugin rate limits.
- Filesystem: read-only ephemeral tmp with zero persistence.
- Persistence: no local disk; persistent work must call host.kv or platform storage APIs (subject to RBAC).

5) Security review & runtime checks
- Static analysis: scan wasm for unsafe imports, suspicious syscalls (try wasm validator + custom rules).
- Signature verification: verify publisher identity and chain.
- Dynamic sandbox: allowlist syscalls, restrict linear memory growth, trap on recursion depth.
- Audit logs: every host.* call emits an audit event.

6) Observability surface
- plugin.metrics: counters, histograms (hosted -> scrub secrets)
- plugin.spans: trace context preserved; plugin should attach span-id to host logs
- plugin.errors: structured error taxonomy (validation, runtime, resource_exhaustion)
- cost accounting: track CPU-ms and charge to route/tenant as part of unit economics

7) Hot vs cold placement strategies
- Inline (in-process isolate) for smallest latency but strict resource micro-limits. Good for tiny formatters.
- Sidecar (separate process/container) for heavier plugins (longer CPU budget, more memory, controlled egress). Scaling: sidecar pool per-route/tenant.
- Warm pools: keep N instances warm for high-QPS routes; fallback to non-plugins when not ready.

Example manifest (text):

# manifest.toml
name = "redwood-formatter"
version = "0.1.2"
entry = "format_response"
capabilities = ["host.log","host.kv-read"]
resource_hints = {cpu_ms = 15, memory_mb = 32, max_qps = 200}
allowed_egress = ["https://api.partner.example"]
publisher = "acme-inc"

Operational notes / open questions:
- Signing: who is the authoritative CA for Hosted plugins? We need an internal publisher registry.
- Threat model: plugin authors might exfiltrate data via outbound requests or timing channels. Mitigations: egress allowlist + throttles + response sampling + strict time budgets.
- Sandbox escape: WASM isolate is strong but many runtimes have host-bindings that are attack surface; minimize host surface area.
- Debugging: how to make developer debugging workable without compromising security? Suggest dev mode where plugin runs with verbose logs only in a dev project.
- Billing: how do we bill for plugin CPU? Per-route CPU-ms with a markup? Need product input.
- Private deployments: customers will want to run their own un-signed plugins. Allowed, but we must provide clear operator guidance and harden telemetry hooks.
- Migration: how to move from ad-hoc server-side middleware -> plugin model? Provide compatibility shim for common JS transforms.

Immediate TODOs:
- prototype loader that verifies manifest + limits memory; test with 3 toy WASM plugins (formatter, rate-limiter, noop) -> team: Ravi
- write static scanner rules for wasm imports and a simple signature verifier -> team: Elena
- draft UX for attaching plugin to route in Console (inline vs sidecar) -> me (Sofia)
- perf tests: 95p latency impact with inline wasm under 1ms target for small formatters

Things to avoid in first rollout:
- No arbitrary outbound network by default in Hosted.
- No KMS access for third-party plugins in Hosted.
- No long-running background threads.

Quick prototyping notes (commands I ran locally):
- wasmtime run --enable-all --invoke format_response plugin.wasm  (toy)
- wasm-validate plugin.wasm  (custom rules)
- small harness: plugin-host.go loads wasm via wasm3, sets up host.* stubs, measures run time

Final thought: prioritize a small, high-safety surface for v1 (formatters, validators). Sidecar + tenant-managed plugins for Dedicated/Private can come later with broader capabilities. Keep UX simple: attach/bind/approve.

Unresolved: permission grant UX (operator vs tenant self-serve), signature CA model, and billing split model.

End of notes.

-- Sofia
